transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Apollo CTO), Ethan Ruiz (Lead Eng), Priya Singh (Product)

Optional summary: quick hosted API walkthrough, show streaming and retries, answer security Qs, agree POC next steps

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm samir with redwood inference, i'll kick us off and lena our se will walk thru a live hosted api demo. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Maya: good, thanks. excited to see streaming — our web chat needs lower perceived latency.
[00:12] Ethan: yep, we get complaints about slow generation on mobile.
[00:15] Samir: great, quick agenda — high level hosted api, then lena will do a live demo of chat generation, show streaming chunks, talk about params like temperature, max_tokens, top_p and then retries and backoff. save q's for end or interrupt. sound ok?
[00:28] Priya: sounds good. can you speak to rate limits / quota too?
[00:32] Samir: yes we'll cover quotas and cost.

--- Demo / Intro
[01:00] Lena: ok i'm going to share my screen — i'll run a small notebook that calls the hosted api. code is python but we also have node examples. first, the simple request: client.chat.create with messages array. system message, user messages, etc. the call returns streaming chunks if you set stream=true.
[01:20] Lena: here's a single-turn example — temperature=0.2, max_tokens=150, top_p=0.95, stop=['\n---'] so you can control creativity and length. when stream=true we send incremental deltas over sse / http2 chunked and the browser can render tokens as they arrive.
[01:40] Ethan: is streaming over websocket or sse?
[01:43] Lena: currently we support server-sent events and chunked http; websockets roadmap but most integrations use sse. latency's typically a few dozen ms per chunk depending on model & sequence length.
[01:55] Maya: and on the client side what code do you recommend to avoid re-assembling partial tokens weirdly?
[02:00] Lena: use the sdk's stream helper that gives you token deltas; for plain sse i usually buffer until you get a token boundary, but the sdk handles that. we also provide examples for streaming in react native which was useful for mobile.

--- Parameters and Examples
[03:10] Lena: quick note on params — temperature controls randomness, 0 is deterministic-ish, 0.7 more varied; top_p is nucleus sampling and can be combined. max_tokens limits generation length. you can also use stop sequences for structured responses. for chat it's common to use system messages to set persona and then user and assistant turns.
[03:40] Priya: for us product-wise we'd like consistent brevity — keep answers 2-3 lines. would setting temperature low and max_tokens 80 be right?
[03:48] Lena: yes that's typical. also you can post-process or set a token budget per request; we can show quotas per route in the console so you can cap spend.

--- Retries and Idempotency
[05:05] Lena: about retries — network errors and 5xx can happen. our recommendation: classify idempotent vs non-idempotent requests. for pure generation you generally treat requests as non-idempotent because the model may produce different outputs, so avoid blind retries without dedup keys. we suggest a request_id header and server-side dedupe for at-least-once semantics. also our sdk exposes a safe_retry helper which does exponential backoff and jitter.
[05:35] Ethan: can you expand on the request_id? we want to avoid duplicate charges and duplicate user-visible responses.
[05:40] Lena: include a client-generated idempotency key in x-request-id; if you re-send with same key within a short window we'll dedupe at the gateway. note: this depends on your retry policy and whether you stream — streaming + retry is trickier, so often clients re-start the request and reconcile on the client with the id. we can share sample patterns.

[07:00] Samir: cost / quotas — hosted is usage-based. tokens in + tokens out count. we can show a sample cost calc in the follow-up email. possible to set per-key quotas and alerting in the console.

--- Security / Compliance Qs
[08:10] Maya: can you confirm data handling? we need SOC2, encryption at rest, and logs for audits.
[08:20] Samir: yes we are SOC2 certified, have encryption at rest and in transit, and you can bring your own KMS for private deployments; for hosted we offer managed KMS but we also support enterprise options. i'll share the SOC2 summary and a security faq.
[08:40] Maya: what about data residency — do you keep data in region?
[08:45] Samir: yes we support region pinning for requests and storage in certain regions; for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private. we'll include region options in the follow-up.

--- Live demo continued (streaming + errors)
[10:00] Lena: i'm going to force a transient error to show retry behavior. here i simulate a 502; the sdk backoff kicks in with exponential backoff (500ms, 1s, 2s) up to configured attempts. if you need deterministic behavior, you can fail-fast and surface an apology message to the user.
[10:35] Ethan: how many retries are default?
[10:38] Lena: default is 3 attempts with jitter; adjustable. we recommend fewer retries for low-latency UI flows.

[12:00] Lena: now streaming live — you can see token deltas coming in, we render as they arrive. here's an example where we stream a long product description: early tokens allow the UI to show skeleton text and reduce perceived latency.
[12:20] Priya: looks snappy. what's the overhead for small responses?
[12:25] Lena: for short responses overhead of chunk negotiation is small; overall token latency dominates. for micro-requests (under 20 tokens) batching can be worse; for large fanout it's good to batch at the gateway.

--- Faults, fallback models, and routing
[14:15] Samir: we also have model routing policies — if a primary model is slow or out of capacity we can fallback to a lower-cost variant automatically. that keeps the user experience up.
[14:30] Maya: interesting — any fine-grained control?
[14:33] Samir: yes you can pin per-route models, set fallback order, and set latency vs cost preference.

--- Questions and competitive notes
[16:10] Ethan: how do you compare to openai in latency?
[16:14] Samir: depends on model, but our hosting and kernel optimizations give comparable or better p50s for common sequence lengths; we also surface per-route latency in the console.
[16:25] Maya: we also evaluate anthopic and aws bedrock — do you have benchmarks?
[16:30] Lena: we have reproducible benchmark sheets; we'll share a trimmed version and the tooling so you can run against your payload.

--- Recap / Next steps
[18:00] Samir: recap — we'll send pricing and a cost model, security docs (SOC2 summary, encryption details), streaming sample code and retry best practices. lena will share the notebook and sdk samples. apollo to confirm dataset for poc and success metrics. schedule POC kickoff for the week of april 6th.
[18:25] Maya: sounds good, thanks. any pricing ballpark now?
[18:30] Samir: i'll include a ballpark in the follow-up; final quote depends on expected qps and retention.
[18:40] Priya: we'll pull together sample convos and traffic profile by friday.

[19:00] Samir: great thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with links to the demo code, security docs, and the pricing sheet.
[19:10] Ethan: thanks, talk soon.

End of recording.
